playground.label: Dates, durations and laps (uses input)
playground.code:
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

text = input('Moment (YYYY/MM/DD HH:MM:SS): ')
moment = datetime.strptime(text, '%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S')
today = datetime(2026, 10, 1, 12, 0, 0)  # a fixed 'now', so every run gives the same lines
wait = moment - today
print('Weekday:', moment.strftime('%A'))
print('Wait:', wait, '=', wait.total_seconds(), 'seconds')
print('1000 days later:', (moment + timedelta(days=1000)).strftime('%B %d, %Y'))

day = moment.date()
found = []
while len(found) < 3:
    day += timedelta(days=1)
    if day.day == 13 and day.weekday() == 4:
        found.append(day.strftime('%B %Y'))
print('Next Friday the 13ths:', ', '.join(found))

# a stopwatch on made-up clock readings, so nothing sleeps
marks = [3.56, 8.63, 17.68, 19.11]
last = 0.0
for n, total in enumerate(marks, 1):
    lap = round(total - last, 2)
    last = total
    print('Lap #' + str(n).rjust(2) + ': ' + str(total).rjust(6) + ' (' + str(lap).rjust(6) + ')')
print(time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time.gmtime(0)))

findings: Background

Chapter 19 of the 3rd edition teaches how a program keeps time, waits, schedules and launches other programs: the time module with the epoch timestamp of time.time(), the text of time.ctime(), profiling by subtracting two timestamps, and time.sleep(); the Super Stopwatch project; the datetime module with datetime objects, fromtimestamp(), comparison, the timedelta type, arithmetic on dates, pausing until a date, and strftime() and strptime() with the directives of Table 19-1; subprocess.run() and subprocess.Popen() with poll(), wait() and kill(), command line arguments, captured output, and opening a file with the start or open command; a pointer to Task Scheduler, launchd and cron; the Simple Countdown project; seven practice questions and two practice programs, the Prettified Stopwatch and the Friday the 13th Finder. The book's chapter ontology models six sections and seven practice questions but not the two projects.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's date and duration arithmetic reproduces under Python 3.14.4: a timedelta of 11 days, 10 hours, 9 minutes and 8 seconds has days 11, seconds 36548 and microseconds 0, total_seconds() 986948.0 and the text 11 days, 10:09:08; 1,000 days after 2 December 2026 at 18:38:50.636181 is 28 August 2029; 21 October 2026 minus 30 times 365 days is 28 October 1996 and minus 60 times that is 5 November 1966; the three strftime() formats and the strptime() parses print what the chapter shows, and the comparisons of the three Halloween and New Year datetimes give the chapter's True, False, True, True.
Comparative analysis

Several printed outputs of the chapter cannot be reproduced as printed because they depend on the time zone of the author's computer: fromtimestamp(1000000) prints 5:46:40 on 12 January 1970, which is the moment in a zone eight hours behind UTC, while the same call gives 13:46:40 in UTC and 15:46:40 on a machine at UTC plus three; time.ctime() formats the local time on a 24-hour clock, so a reading at 11:04 PM prints 23:04 and not the 11:05:38 the chapter shows; and the chapter's timestamp 1773813875 is 23:04:35 on 17 March 2026 in Pacific Daylight Time (UTC minus 7), although the chapter says Pacific Standard Time.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's rule for two-digit years is wrong by one: the text and Table 19-1 say %y spans 1970 to 2069, but the documentation and the interpreter map the values 69 to 99 to 1969 to 1999 and the values 0 to 68 to 2000 to 2068, so strptime() reads 69 as 1969 and 68 as 2068; the chapter's own examples, 63 as 2063 and 73 as 1973, are right under either rule.
Comparative analysis

Four listings of the chapter as served on its web page contain the typographic en dash in place of the minus sign (end_time – start_time, time.time() – last_time twice, and oct_21st – about_thirty_years), which Python rejects with a SyntaxError that names the character, U+2013; the Windows example that opens hello.txt writes 'C:\\Users\Al\\hello.txt' with an unescaped backslash before the A, which current Python compiles with a SyntaxWarning about an invalid escape sequence, the warning that has existed since Python 3.12 and is planned to become an error; and the prose calls datetime.timedelta() datetime.delta(), a name the module does not have.
Comparative analysis

The chapter profiles code by subtracting two time.time() readings, and the documentation adds why that is fragile: time.time() reads the system clock, which can be set back so that a later call returns a smaller value, while time.monotonic() and time.perf_counter() are monotonic clocks that cannot go backwards and are not affected by clock updates, so only a difference of two readings is meaningful and the difference is the right measure of a duration; the chapter's calcProd.py also forms a product with 1,516,705 bits, and printing it fails under the default limit of 4300 digits for integer to text conversion that Python has had since 3.11, a limit the chapter does not meet because it prints only the elapsed time.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's claim that time.sleep() pauses a program for the given number of seconds is sharpened by the documentation: since Python 3.5 a sleep interrupted by a signal is restarted, so it lasts at least the requested time, but it may last longer by an arbitrary amount because of scheduling; since 3.11 it uses clock_nanosleep() or nanosleep() on Unix; and the chapter's loop that sleeps one second and compares datetime.now() with a target compares naive local times, which a change of the computer's clock or its daylight saving rules moves, so a long wait is better handed to the operating system's scheduler, as the chapter itself advises.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's subprocess account holds and current Python adds to it: run() waits and returns a CompletedProcess whose text form lists the arguments and the return code and, when output was captured, the captured text; a program that cannot be found raises FileNotFoundError; check=True turns a nonzero exit code into CalledProcessError and timeout= kills the child and raises TimeoutExpired; a Popen object's poll() returns None while the child runs and the exit code afterwards, kill() ends the child so that its return code is -9 on Linux (a negative value means a signal), and the documentation warns that wait() can deadlock when the child's output goes to a pipe that nobody reads; none of the chapter's Windows and macOS launches of Calculator, Paint and Notepad could be run, because they need those programs and a screen.
Conclusion

For an advanced course, chapter 19 is best taught as the choice of a clock by the question asked and of a launcher by the question asked: a wall-clock moment is a datetime (aware, in a zone), a duration measured on the machine is a monotonic or performance counter difference, a duration between moments is a timedelta, and a program is launched with a list of arguments through run() or, when it must run alongside, Popen; the chapter's date arithmetic holds under 3.14.4, and the zone dependence of its printed times, the two-digit year range, the en dash and backslash slips, the monotonic clocks, aware datetimes and zoneinfo, the year-less parsing warning, security of shell=True, and in-process scheduling are what the chapter leaves for the course to add.
Contemporary developments

Current Python deprecates the datetime call the old idiom relied on and gives the tools the chapter leaves out: datetime.utcnow() and utcfromtimestamp() have raised a DeprecationWarning since 3.12 in favour of datetime.now(datetime.UTC); a datetime is naive or aware according to its tzinfo, a naive and an aware value are never equal and cannot be ordered; the zoneinfo module supplies IANA zones; adding a timedelta to an aware datetime in one zone moves the wall-clock time, so one day added across the start of daylight saving time is 23 hours of elapsed time; and the fold attribute of PEP 495 tells apart the two passes through a repeated hour.
Contemporary developments

Parsing a month and a day without a year has changed: since Python 3.13 strptime() emits a DeprecationWarning because the default year 1900 is not a leap year, so '02 29' fails, and the documentation says such formats may raise an error as of Python 3.15; the remedy is to include a year, and Python 3.14 adds date.strptime() and time.strptime() beside datetime.strptime().
Contemporary developments

The chapter's advice to open a file with start or open and its use of shell=True on Windows meet a security rule of the documentation: a list of arguments is passed to the program without a shell, so spaces and metacharacters are safe, whereas with shell=True the program must quote every piece of text itself, for which shlex.quote() exists on POSIX; text joined into a shell command runs as two commands, and quoted it does not; the webbrowser module's open() and, on Windows only, os.startfile() are the documentation's ways to open a page or a file with its default program, and none of them was run here.
Contemporary developments

The chapter hands scheduling to Task Scheduler, launchd and cron, which run programs even when no Python program is alive; the standard library offers only in-process scheduling that ends with the program: sched.scheduler runs events in order of time and then priority (a lower number first) with a clock and a delay function that can be replaced, and threading.Timer runs a function after a delay in a thread and can be cancelled before it fires.
title: Keeping time, scheduling tasks and launching programs for an advanced course: chapter 19 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Time module
nodes.body: The time module reads the system clock, measures stretches of time and pauses a program, and is the first half of the chapter (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Measure and pause
nodes.body: The time module measures how long code takes and pauses a program (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Elapsed time
nodes.body: The chapter profiles calculate_product() by calling time.time() before and after it and subtracting, and the printed seconds differ from machine to machine, so the book's 2.844162940979004 is one machine's reading (Sweigart, 2025); the listing as served on the chapter page writes the subtraction with an en dash, end_time – start_time, which Python rejects with a SyntaxError naming the character U+2013 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Elapsed time is the difference of two clock readings taken before and after a block of code, which is how the chapter profiles calculate_product().

nodes.label: Monotonic clock
nodes.body: time.time() can return a smaller value than a previous call if the system clock was set back, while time.monotonic() and time.perf_counter() cannot go backwards and are not affected by clock updates, and only the difference between two of their readings means anything (Simpson et al., 2012) (Python Software Foundation, 2026); time.get_clock_info reports time as not monotonic and adjustable, and monotonic and perf_counter as monotonic and not adjustable; the chapter's product of the first 100,000 numbers has 1,516,705 bits, and converting it to text fails with ValueError under the default limit of 4300 digits, so a program that prints it must raise the limit (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A monotonic clock cannot go backwards and is not changed when someone sets the system clock, so the difference of two of its readings is a reliable duration; time.time() is a clock that can be set.

nodes.label: Round function
nodes.body: round(4.766272783279419, 2) is 4.77, the chapter's example of trimming a long float, and the answer to practice question 5: round returns the number rounded to the digits given, and with no digits it returns an int, rounding a half to the even neighbour, so round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4; str(round(3.5, 2)) is '3.5' and not '3.50', which matters when the chapter's lap times are lined up (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: round returns its number rounded to the digits asked for, and with no digits it returns an integer, rounding halves to the even neighbour.

nodes.label: Sleep function
nodes.body: time.sleep(seconds) blocks the program, so the prompt of the interactive shell does not return until the time has passed, and a while loop that sleeps one second and compares datetime.now() with a target pauses until a date (Sweigart, 2025); since Python 3.5 a sleep interrupted by a signal is restarted, so it lasts at least the time asked, it may last longer, and from 3.11 it uses clock_nanosleep or nanosleep on Unix (Natali and Stinner, 2014) (Python Software Foundation, 2026); started on 1 October 2026, the chapter's loop that waits for Halloween 2039 would wait 4778 days (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: time.sleep blocks the calling program for at least the given number of seconds, so a loop that checks the clock once a second does not burn processor time.

nodes.label: Epoch clock text
nodes.body: The chapter's first clock counts seconds since one fixed moment and can show that count as text (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Epoch timestamp
nodes.body: The Unix epoch is midnight on 1 January 1970 in UTC, time.time() returns the seconds since it as a float, called an epoch timestamp, and the chapter's example value is 1773813875.3518236 (Sweigart, 2025); time.gmtime(0) is the epoch itself, (1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0) in its first six fields, and the reading time.time() is a float (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The time module counts seconds since the Unix epoch, midnight on 1 January 1970 in UTC, and time.time() returns that count as a float, called an epoch timestamp.

nodes.label: Readable time string
nodes.body: time.ctime() gives a text for the current moment or for a given epoch timestamp (Sweigart, 2025); the text is in the computer's local time, so it depends on the time zone, and it uses a 24-hour clock, which is why the chapter's 'Tue Mar 17 11:05:38 2026', said to be read at 11 PM, cannot be what ctime printed: with the time zone set to America/Los_Angeles ctime(1773813875.3518236) prints 'Tue Mar 17 23:04:35 2026', in Europe/Istanbul it prints 'Wed Mar 18 09:04:35 2026' and in UTC 'Wed Mar 18 06:04:35 2026'; time.asctime(time.gmtime(1773813875)) gives the UTC text in every zone (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: time.ctime turns an epoch timestamp, or the current moment, into a text such as 'Wed Mar 18 06:04:35 2026' in the computer's local time on a 24-hour clock.

nodes.label: Local versus utc
nodes.body: datetime.fromtimestamp(1000000) in the chapter prints 1970-01-12 05:46:40, the clock reading in a zone eight hours behind UTC; the same timestamp is 13:46:40 in UTC and 15:46:40 in a zone three hours ahead, so the chapter's printed value is reproducible only with its zone stated, and the chapter's 1773813875 is 23:04:35 on 17 March 2026 in Pacific Daylight Time, UTC minus 7, although the chapter calls it Pacific Standard Time (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Converting an epoch timestamp to a date gives a different clock reading in each time zone for the same moment, so a printed time is reproducible only with its zone stated.

nodes.label: Datetime module
nodes.body: The datetime module holds moments and durations, does arithmetic on them and converts them to and from text, and is the second half of the time part of the chapter (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Moments and ordering
nodes.body: A datetime object is the chapter's value for a specific moment (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Datetime object
nodes.body: datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 16, 29, 0) stores 2026, 10, 21, 16, 29 and 0 in the attributes year, month, day, hour, minute and second, hour, minute and second default to 0, and the object also has microsecond (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A datetime object holds a moment as year, month, day, hour, minute, second and microsecond, with hour, minute and second defaulting to 0.

nodes.label: Current moment
nodes.body: datetime.datetime.now() returns the current moment as a naive datetime and datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(time.time()) does the same, the two differing by less than a second when called together (Sweigart, 2025); datetime.now(datetime.UTC) returns an aware value whose offset from UTC is timedelta(0) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: datetime.now returns the current moment according to the computer's clock as a value with no time zone attached, unless a zone is passed.

nodes.label: Datetime comparison
nodes.body: With halloween_2026 and oct_31_2026 both at midnight on 31 October 2026 and new_years_2027 at midnight on 1 January 2027, halloween_2026 == oct_31_2026 is True, halloween_2026 > new_years_2027 is False, new_years_2027 > halloween_2026 is True and new_years_2027 != oct_31_2026 is True (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Datetime values are compared with the usual operators, and the later moment is the greater one.

io.code: (lambda d, h, n: (h == d(2026, 10, 31), h > n, n > h))(__import__('datetime').datetime, __import__('datetime').datetime(2026, 10, 31), __import__('datetime').datetime(2027, 1, 1))

nodes.label: Duration measures
nodes.body: A timedelta is the chapter's value for an amount of time (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Timedelta object
nodes.body: timedelta(days=11, hours=10, minutes=9, seconds=8) has days 11, seconds 36548, which is 10 hours, 9 minutes and 8 seconds in seconds, and microseconds 0 (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A timedelta holds a duration, not a moment, normalised into days, seconds and microseconds.

nodes.label: Duration readouts
nodes.body: total_seconds() of that duration is 986948.0 and str() of it is '11 days, 10:09:08' (Sweigart, 2025); a negative duration is normalised so that timedelta(days=-1, seconds=1) prints as '-1 day, 0:00:01' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: total_seconds returns the whole duration as a float number of seconds and str gives a text such as '11 days, 10:09:08'.

nodes.label: Duration units
nodes.body: timedelta takes weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds and microseconds, so timedelta(weeks=1, hours=24) is 8 days, and it takes no months or years because those vary in length, which timedelta(months=1) confirms by raising TypeError (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026); the chapter's prose calls the constructor datetime.delta(), a name the module does not have (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A timedelta takes weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds and microseconds but no months or years, because those have no fixed length.

nodes.label: Date arithmetic
nodes.body: Datetime and timedelta values are combined with the arithmetic operators (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Add subtract duration
nodes.body: Adding timedelta(days=1000) to 2 December 2026 at 18:38:50.636181 gives 28 August 2029 at the same time, and subtracting about thirty years, timedelta(days=365 * 30), from 21 October 2026 at 16:29 gives 28 October 1996, and subtracting twice that gives 5 November 1966, a little off the same date thirty years back because the chapter ignores leap years; the chapter's listing as served writes that subtraction with an en dash, which is a SyntaxError (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A timedelta is added to or subtracted from a datetime with + and -, multiplied by a number with *, and the module handles month lengths and leap years.

nodes.label: Date difference
nodes.body: Subtracting two datetimes gives a timedelta, so midnight on 1 January 2027 minus midnight on 31 October 2026 is 62 days, and the same subtraction is how a countdown finds the time left to a future moment (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Subtracting one datetime from another gives a timedelta, the time between the two moments.

nodes.label: Weekday of date
nodes.body: Practice question 7 asks the weekday of 7 January 2019: datetime.date(2019, 1, 7).strftime('%A') is 'Monday' and its weekday() is 0, since weekday() counts Monday as 0 (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The weekday of a date is found by formatting it with %A for its name or by calling weekday(), which counts Monday as 0.

nodes.label: Format parse
nodes.body: strftime turns a datetime into text and strptime turns text into a datetime, both with the directives of Table 19-1 (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Strftime format
nodes.body: For 21 October 2026 at 16:29, strftime('%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S') is '2026/10/21 16:29:00', strftime('%I:%M %p') is '04:29 PM', the format %B of '%y gives the text October of '26, and the directives %j, %w, %A, %a, %b, %d, %% and %y give '294', '3', 'Wednesday', 'Wed', 'Oct', '21', '%' and '26' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: strftime returns a datetime as text from a format string of directives such as %Y, %m, %d, %H, %M, %S, %I and %p.

nodes.label: Strptime parse
nodes.body: strptime('October 21, 2026', '%B %d, %Y') is datetime(2026, 10, 21, 0, 0), strptime('2026/10/21 16:29:00', '%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S') is 21 October 2026 at 16:29, and reading the text October of '26 with the format %B of '%y gives 1 October 2026, the missing day defaulting to 1 (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: strptime is the inverse of strftime: it reads a datetime from text with a format string of the same directives.

nodes.label: Two digit year
nodes.body: The chapter says %y spans 1970 to 2069, but the interpreter and the documentation map 69 to 99 to 1969 to 1999 and 0 to 68 to 2000 to 2068, so strptime reads the years 68, 69, 70 as 2068, 1969, 1970 and the chapter's examples, November of '63 as 2063 and November of '73 as 1973, hold under either rule (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The %y directive reads a two-digit year by the rule that 69 to 99 mean 1969 to 1999 and 0 to 68 mean 2000 to 2068.

nodes.label: Parse mismatch
nodes.body: A text that does not match the format exactly raises ValueError, for example '2026-10-21' against '%Y/%m/%d' gives the message time data '2026-10-21' does not match format '%Y/%m/%d', and 'Oct 21, 2026' against '%B %d, %Y' fails because %B wants the full month name (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A text that does not match the format exactly raises ValueError.

nodes.label: Zone rules
nodes.body: Beyond the chapter, a datetime may carry a time zone, and the zone decides what the arithmetic means (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Naive versus aware
nodes.body: datetime(2026, 10, 21).tzinfo is None, so it is naive, and the same value with tzinfo=datetime.UTC is aware; a naive and an aware value are never equal, and ordering them with < raises TypeError with the message can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes; datetime.UTC is datetime.timezone.utc (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A datetime without a tzinfo is naive and one with a tzinfo is aware; naive and aware values are never equal and cannot be ordered.

nodes.label: Utcnow deprecated
nodes.body: datetime.utcnow() and datetime.utcfromtimestamp() each raise a DeprecationWarning under Python 3.14.4, since they were deprecated in 3.12, and the replacement is datetime.now(datetime.UTC) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: datetime.utcnow and utcfromtimestamp return naive values and have been deprecated since Python 3.12 in favour of aware values made with datetime.UTC.

nodes.label: Zone info zones
nodes.body: With zoneinfo, fromtimestamp(1773813875, ZoneInfo('America/Los_Angeles')) is 2026-03-17T23:04:35-07:00 with the zone name PDT, which settles the chapter's 'Pacific Standard Time'; the module uses the system's zone database or the tzdata package, and is not available on WebAssembly platforms, so it was executed natively and not in the page (Ganssle, 2020) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The zoneinfo module attaches an IANA time zone, with its daylight saving rules, to a datetime as its tzinfo.

nodes.label: Wall clock arithmetic
nodes.body: For 12:00 on 7 March 2026 in America/Los_Angeles, adding timedelta(days=1) gives 12:00 on 8 March at offset -07:00 and the difference of the two is 1 day, but converted to UTC the two moments are 23 hours apart because daylight saving time began that day; the fold attribute of PEP 495 tells the two passes through the repeated hour apart, so 1:30 on 1 November 2026 has offset -7 hours with fold 0 and -8 hours with fold 1 (Belopolsky and Peters, 2015) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Adding a duration to an aware datetime in one zone moves the wall-clock reading, so adding one day across the start of daylight saving time spans 23 hours.

nodes.label: Yearless parsing
nodes.body: strptime('02 28', '%m %d') gives 28 February 1900 and a DeprecationWarning, strptime('02 29', '%m %d') raises ValueError because 1900 has no 29 February, and adding a leap year to text and format, '02/29;1984' with '%m/%d;%Y', gives 29 February 1984; the documentation says such formats may raise an error as of Python 3.15, and Python 3.14 adds date.strptime and time.strptime, so date.strptime('2026-10-21', '%Y-%m-%d') is datetime.date(2026, 10, 21) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Parsing a month and a day without a year uses the non-leap year 1900, which fails for 29 February and draws a DeprecationWarning since Python 3.13; adding a leap year to the text and the format avoids it.

nodes.label: Launching programs
nodes.body: The subprocess module starts other programs from Python and is the last part of the chapter (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Run a program
nodes.body: subprocess.run starts a program and waits for it (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Run function
nodes.body: subprocess.run(['/usr/bin/gnome-calculator']) waits until the calculator closes and then returns CompletedProcess(args=[...], returncode=0), which is also what the chapter prints for Windows and macOS (Sweigart, 2025); none of those launches was run here, because they need those programs and a screen, and a run of the current Python interpreter instead printed CompletedProcess with the arguments and the return code 0; the subprocess module does not work on WebAssembly, so the page shows only the parts of these examples that start no program (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: subprocess.run starts another program, waits until it ends and returns a CompletedProcess that records the arguments and the return code.

nodes.label: Argument list
nodes.body: Passing the program and its arguments as a list means the launched program sees them as its sys.argv, so ['notepad', 'hello.txt'] opens hello.txt, and a run of the interpreter with the arguments 'hello.txt' and 'two words' received exactly those two arguments, the second with its space; the documentation prefers a list to a single string, and shlex.split turns the shell-style text notepad hello.txt 'my file.txt' into the list ['notepad', 'hello.txt', 'my file.txt'] (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The program and its command line arguments are given as a list of strings, the first being the program, so a file name with spaces stays one argument.

nodes.label: Capture output
nodes.body: capture_output=True and text=True keep the program's output as a string in the stdout attribute, which the chapter uses to read the output of ping; a run of the interpreter printing hi gave stdout 'hi\n', empty stderr and return code 0, and without text=True the output is bytes, b'hi\n'; the ping example needs the network and its Windows output was not run (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: With capture_output=True the text the program prints is kept in the stdout and stderr attributes of the result, as text when text=True and as bytes otherwise.

nodes.label: Exit code
nodes.body: An exit code of 0 means success and another value means failure; a child that ended with sys.exit(3) gave returncode 3 (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An exit code of 0 means the program ended without error and any other value that it failed; a negative value means a signal ended it.

nodes.label: Check and timeout
nodes.body: With check=True a child exiting with code 2 raised CalledProcessError, with timeout=0.3 a child sleeping 5 seconds was killed and raised TimeoutExpired, and a program name that does not exist raised FileNotFoundError; the chapter mentions none of these (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: check=True raises CalledProcessError on a nonzero exit code and timeout kills the program and raises TimeoutExpired when it runs too long; a program that does not exist raises FileNotFoundError.

nodes.label: Process controls
nodes.body: subprocess.Popen returns an object for a program that runs alongside the Python program (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Popen launch
nodes.body: Popen starts the program and continues without waiting, unlike run, and the chapter notes that on Windows 10 and later calc.exe hands over to the Calculator app and ends at once, so wait() returns immediately; the chapter's Popen calls on Calculator and Paint were not run here (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Popen starts a program and returns at once with an object for the running process, so the Python program continues alongside it.

nodes.label: Poll and wait
nodes.body: For a child that sleeps 0.4 seconds, poll() returned None while it ran, and after wait() both wait() and poll() gave 0; the Popen class has the methods poll, wait, kill, terminate and communicate, and the documentation warns that wait() can deadlock when the child's output goes to a pipe that is not read, for which communicate() is the remedy (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: poll asks whether the process has ended without waiting, returning None while it runs and the exit code afterwards, and wait blocks until it ends and returns the exit code.

io.code: [m for m in ('poll', 'wait', 'kill', 'terminate', 'communicate') if hasattr(__import__('subprocess').Popen, m)]

nodes.label: Kill process
nodes.body: kill() ended a child that would have slept 30 seconds, after which poll() and wait() gave -9, a negative return code meaning signal 9; on POSIX kill sends SIGKILL and on Windows it is an alias for terminate (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: kill ends the process at once, without asking it to save, so its unsaved work is lost.

nodes.label: Open with shell
nodes.body: The chapter opens files and pages with the program the system associates with them (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Default application
nodes.body: subprocess.run(['start', 'hello.txt'], shell=True) on Windows and subprocess.run(['open', 'hello.txt']) on macOS ask the operating system to open the file with its associated program; the commands depend on the platform, were not run here, and the chapter's own Simple Countdown project uses them with an alarm.wav file (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The start command on Windows and the open command on macOS open a file with the program the operating system associates with its type.

nodes.label: Shell true
nodes.body: With shell=True the text goes to the system shell: 'echo hi && echo there' printed two lines, and 'echo x; echo INJECTED' run as shell text ran a second command, while the same text quoted with shlex.quote, 'x; echo INJECTED' as one word, did not; the documentation says that with shell=True the program must quote everything itself (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: With shell=True the text is run by the system shell, so a program must quote any outside text in it itself, for example with shlex.quote, or the text can run extra commands.

nodes.label: Browser open
nodes.body: webbrowser.open(url, new=0, autoraise=True) shows a page in the default browser and returns True if one was launched, the chapter suggests it for an alarm that opens a website; it was not run here because it needs a browser and a screen (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: webbrowser.open shows a page in the default browser and returns True if a browser was launched.

nodes.label: Scheduling
nodes.body: A program can wait for a time itself or hand the time to something else (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Scheduling tools
nodes.body: The chapter sends long waits to the operating system and short waits to a sleeping loop (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Os scheduler
nodes.body: Task Scheduler on Windows, launchd on macOS and cron on Linux start programs at chosen times and are the chapter's advice for a program that must start at a set time, since a sleeping Python program has to stay alive; they were read from the chapter and not run here (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The operating system's own scheduler starts a program at chosen times even when no Python program is running, which a Python program that sleeps cannot do.

nodes.label: Sched module
nodes.body: sched.scheduler with a fake clock that starts at 0 and a delay function that advances it ran an event entered at delay 5 after one entered at delay 2, gave the order 'two-first', 'two', 'five' for a priority-0 and a priority-1 event at the same time and one at 5, and ended at clock time 5, so a lower priority number runs first among events at the same time (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: sched.scheduler runs functions at given times inside one running program, in the order of time and then priority, with a replaceable clock and delay function.

io.code: (lambda log, clock: (lambda s: (s.enter(5, 1, log.append, ('five',)), s.enter(2, 1, log.append, ('two',)), s.run(), log)[-1])(__import__('sched').scheduler(lambda: clock[0], lambda d: clock.__setitem__(0, clock[0] + d))))([], [0])

steps.expr: (lambda log, clock: (lambda s: (s.enter(5, 1, log.append, ('five',)), s.enter(2, 1, log.append, ('two',)), s.run(), log)[-1])(__import__('sched').scheduler(lambda: clock[0], lambda d: clock.__setitem__(0, clock[0] + d))))([], [0])

nodes.label: Timer thread
nodes.body: threading.Timer(0.05, f) ran f once after the delay in a thread and Timer(5, f) cancelled before it fired never ran; Timer is a subclass of Thread and, like sched, lives and dies with the program (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: threading.Timer runs a function once after a delay in a thread of its own, and cancel stops it while it is still waiting.

nodes.label: Projects
nodes.body: The chapter has two projects and two practice programs that use the clock (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Stopwatch program
nodes.body: The Super Stopwatch and its prettified form time laps (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Lap timing
nodes.body: The stopwatch stores start_time and last_time, each press of Enter gives lap_time as now minus last_time and total_time as now minus start_time, both rounded with round(..., 2), so totals 3.56, 8.63 and 17.68 give laps 3.56, 5.07 and 9.05; the listing as served writes these subtractions with an en dash, which is a SyntaxError, and time.monotonic() would be the clock to use (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The stopwatch keeps the time of the start and of the last lap, and each lap time is the difference from the last lap and each total the difference from the start.

nodes.label: Prettified laps
nodes.body: The Prettified Stopwatch pads the lap number to 2 characters and each time to 6 with rjust, so the lap lines are 'Lap # 1:   3.56 (  3.56)', 'Lap # 2:   8.63 (  5.07)', 'Lap # 3:  17.68 (  9.05)' and 'Lap # 4:  19.11 (  1.43)', as the chapter asks; str(round(x, 2)) drops a trailing zero, so a time of 5.0 shows as 5.0 and a format such as {:>6.2f} keeps two decimals; the chapter also asks for pyperclip, which was not run (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: rjust pads a text on the left to a fixed width, so the lap numbers and times line up in columns.

nodes.label: Interrupt to stop
nodes.body: Ctrl-C raises KeyboardInterrupt inside input(), the stopwatch catches it and prints Done.; KeyboardInterrupt is a BaseException and not an Exception, so an except Exception clause would not catch it, and the project's input() was not run interactively here (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Pressing Ctrl-C raises KeyboardInterrupt, which the stopwatch catches to end quietly; it is a subclass of BaseException and not of Exception.

nodes.label: Countdown program
nodes.body: The Simple Countdown waits and then plays a sound (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Countdown loop
nodes.body: With time_left = 60 the loop prints 60 down to 1, sleeping one second after each, and then runs an alarm; with 5 it prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1; the chapter's alarm.wav is opened with start or open, which was not run here, and the chapter points to playsound3 in another chapter (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The countdown prints the seconds left, sleeps one second and subtracts one until none is left, and then runs the alarm.

nodes.label: Time until event
nodes.body: For a long countdown the chapter suggests a timedelta to a future moment, for example midnight on 1 January 2027 minus 12:00 on 1 October 2026, which is '91 days, 12:00:00' (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A long countdown is the timedelta between now and a future moment.

nodes.label: Friday thirteenth program
nodes.body: The Friday the 13th Finder is the chapter's practice program for dates (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Forward search
nodes.body: Starting on 1 October 2026 and adding one day at a time, the first ten dates with day 13 and weekday Friday are November 2026, August 2027, October 2028, April 2029, July 2029, September 2030, December 2030, June 2031, February 2032 and August 2032 (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The forward finder starts at a date and adds one day at a time, printing the month and year of each date whose day is 13 and whose weekday is Friday, until it has ten.

io.code: [d.isoformat() for d in (__import__('datetime').date(2026, 10, 1) + __import__('datetime').timedelta(days=n) for n in range(400)) if d.day == 13 and d.weekday() == 4]

nodes.label: Backward search
nodes.body: Subtracting one day at a time from 1 October 2026 finds 3485 such dates before the start, the earliest on 13 April of year 1 and the latest on 13 March 2026, and the next subtraction from 0001-01-01 raises OverflowError with the message date value out of range, which is how the loop learns to stop (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The backward finder subtracts one day at a time and must stop at year 1, because subtracting a day from the earliest date raises OverflowError.

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition: Chapter 19, Keeping Time, Scheduling Tasks, and Launching Programs
resources.why: The course textbook's own chapter, free online: the time and datetime modules, subprocess, the stopwatch and countdown projects, and the practice questions.

resources.title: time — Time access and conversions
resources.why: Every clock in the time module with the clock it reads: time, monotonic, perf_counter, sleep, ctime, and the rule that maps %y to 1969-2068.

resources.title: datetime — Basic date and time types
resources.why: The reference for datetime, timedelta, aware and naive values, and the table of strftime and strptime directives.

resources.title: subprocess — Subprocess management
resources.why: run, CompletedProcess, Popen with poll, wait and kill, and the security considerations for shell=True.

resources.title: sched — Event scheduler
resources.why: The in-process scheduler: events ordered by time and then priority, with a clock and a delay function you can replace.

resources.title: threading — Thread-based parallelism
resources.why: Timer objects, which run a function once after a delay and can be cancelled while they wait.

resources.title: zoneinfo — IANA time zone support
resources.why: Attaching a named time zone to a datetime, and how daylight saving time changes the arithmetic.

resources.title: shlex — Simple lexical analysis
resources.why: split, quote and join: turning shell-style text into an argument list and quoting text for a shell.

resources.title: webbrowser — Convenient web-browser controller
resources.why: open, open_new and open_new_tab: showing a page in the default browser.

resources.title: PEP 418 – Add monotonic time, performance counter, and process time functions
resources.why: Why time.monotonic and time.perf_counter were added: a program that times or schedules with the system clock fails when the clock is set.

resources.title: PEP 615 – Support for the IANA Time Zone Database in the Standard Library
resources.why: Why the zoneinfo module exists and how it attaches named zones to datetimes.

resources.title: Python Tutor
resources.why: Paste a program and step through it line by line, for example the stopwatch or the Friday the 13th loop, to see each value change.
